title: Power of data in quantum machine learning
authors: Huang, H.-Y., Broughton, M., Mohseni, M., Babbush, R., Boixo, S., Neven, H., McClean, J. R.
idea: Quantum ML models do not automatically outperform classical ones. By carefully constructing classical kernels that mimic quantum feature maps, classical ML can match or exceed quantum models on most practical datasets. The key insight is that quantum advantage in ML requires data with genuine quantum structure.
takeaway: Quantum advantage in ML requires problem structure that genuinely cannot be captured classically. Such structure is rare in current benchmarks and unlikely to appear in standard industrial datasets.

title: Cost function dependent barren plateaus in shallow parametrized quantum circuits
authors: Cerezo, M., Sone, A., Volkoff, T., Cincio, L., Coles, P. J.
idea: Barren plateaus depend critically on whether the cost function is global or local. Local cost functions on shallow circuits can avoid barren plateaus even at scale, providing a partial path forward for trainable VQAs.
takeaway: Choosing the right loss function is as important as choosing the ansatz. Global cost functions are untrainable at scale; local ones are not, but they introduce other expressibility trade-offs.

title: Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes
authors: McClean, J. R., Boixo, S., Smelyanskiy, V. N., Babbush, R., Neven, H.
idea: For random parametrized quantum circuits, the gradient of the cost function vanishes exponentially in the number of qubits. This makes training quantum neural networks on random initializations effectively impossible at scale.
takeaway: The foundational barren plateau paper. Essential reading before designing any variational quantum algorithm. The result is not a bug to fix — it is a fundamental property of high-dimensional quantum state spaces.

title: Quantum Computing in the NISQ Era and Beyond
authors: Preskill, J.
idea: NISQ devices with 50-100 noisy qubits may achieve tasks beyond classical simulation but fault-tolerant quantum computing remains a long-term goal. The term NISQ was coined here to frame realistic near-term expectations.
takeaway: The essential framing paper for modern quantum computing. Understanding what NISQ means — and what it does not promise — is prerequisite knowledge for evaluating any quantum hardware claim.

title: Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor
authors: Arute, F., Arya, K., Babbush, R. et al. (Google AI Quantum)
idea: Google 53-qubit Sycamore processor completed a specific random circuit sampling task in 200 seconds, estimated to take 10,000 years on the best classical supercomputer at the time. A landmark but contested result.
takeaway: Landmark but contested. The task was artificial, IBM later disputed the classical simulation estimate, and the result demonstrates quantum supremacy for a specific useless task rather than practical advantage. Essential for understanding benchmarking pitfalls.

title: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
authors: Gidney, C., Ekera, M.
idea: A detailed resource estimation for running Shor's algorithm at practical scale. Breaking RSA-2048 requires approximately 20 million physical qubits running for 8 hours with surface code error correction at realistic error rates.
takeaway: The definitive paper for realistic Shor's algorithm resource estimates. Whenever someone claims quantum computers will soon break encryption, this paper shows the actual hardware gap. Current best hardware has around 1000 qubits.

title: Expressibility and entangling capability of parametrized quantum circuits for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms
authors: Sim, S., Johnson, P. D., Aspuru-Guzik, A.
idea: Introduces quantitative measures for comparing parametrized quantum circuit designs — expressibility (how much of Hilbert space the ansatz can reach) and entangling capability (how much entanglement it generates on average).
takeaway: Gives researchers a principled way to compare ansatz designs instead of relying on intuition. Shows the fundamental trade-off: high expressibility correlates with poor trainability (barren plateaus).

title: A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: Farhi, E., Goldstone, J., Gutmann, S.
idea: Introduces QAOA — a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for combinatorial optimization. Alternates between a problem Hamiltonian and a mixing Hamiltonian for p layers to approximate optimal solutions, with approximation ratio improving with p.
takeaway: One of the most studied near-term quantum algorithms. The approximation ratio for p=1 QAOA on MaxCut gives roughly 0.69 — better than random but worse than the best classical approximation algorithms for many problem instances.

title: A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search
authors: Grover, L. K.
journal: Proceedings of the 28th Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing
idea: A quantum computer can search an unsorted database of N items in O(sqrt(N)) queries instead of O(N) classically, using amplitude amplification. This is a provably optimal quadratic speedup for unstructured search.
takeaway: Quadratic, not exponential speedup. It works through interference, not parallel search. Bennett et al. (1997) proved this speedup is optimal — no quantum algorithm can do better for unstructured search.

title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer
authors: Shor, P. W.
idea: A quantum computer can factor large integers in polynomial time using quantum Fourier transform and period finding — exponentially faster than the best known classical algorithms. This breaks RSA but requires fault-tolerant hardware far beyond current capability.
takeaway: The most famous quantum algorithm. Breaks RSA in principle but requires millions of error-corrected qubits. The algorithm is theoretically settled — the challenge is entirely hardware.

title: Quantum machine learning
authors: Biamonte, J., Wittek, P., Pancotti, N., Rebentrost, P., Wiebe, N., Lloyd, S.
idea: A review of the intersection of quantum computing and machine learning — covering quantum-enhanced ML algorithms, quantum neural networks, and the fundamental challenges of loading classical data into quantum systems.
takeaway: The accessible entry point to QML. Covers the landscape including both the promises and the serious caveats around data loading. Essential first read before the more critical papers.

title: A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems
authors: Tang, E.
journal: Proceedings of the 51st Annual ACM STOC
idea: Shows that a quantum algorithm for recommendation systems claimed to give exponential speedup can be matched by a classical algorithm using quantum-inspired sampling techniques. This dequantization result triggered a re-evaluation of many proposed quantum ML speedups.
takeaway: A watershed paper. Many proposed quantum ML speedups were based on assumptions about data access that, if provided to classical algorithms, remove the quantum advantage. Demonstrated that quantum advantage claims require careful analysis of the classical baseline.

title: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
authors: Fowler, A. M., Martinis, J. M., Martinis, A., Whiteside, A., Whiteside, J.
idea: A comprehensive treatment of surface codes — the leading quantum error correction approach for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing. Shows that with physical error rates below 1%, logical error rates can be made arbitrarily small by increasing code distance.
takeaway: The definitive surface code reference. Explains why error correction requires roughly 1000 physical qubits per logical qubit at realistic error rates and what engineering challenges must be solved for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic chip
authors: Peruzzo, A., McClean, J., Shadbolt, P., Yung, M.-H., Zhou, X.-Q., Love, P. J., Aspuru-Guzik, A., OBrien, J. L.
idea: Introduces the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) — a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for finding the ground state energy of quantum systems. First demonstrated on a photonic chip for a simple molecule.
takeaway: The foundational VQE paper. VQE is the most widely studied near-term quantum algorithm for quantum chemistry. However, classical simulation of small molecules remains competitive and VQE scaling to practically useful problems remains unproven.

title: Parameterized quantum circuits as machine learning models
authors: Benedetti, M., Lloyd, E., Sack, S., Fiorentini, M.
idea: A systematic review of parametrized quantum circuits as machine learning models, covering training strategies, expressibility, gradient computation methods including the parameter shift rule, and practical implementation considerations.
takeaway: The most practical reference for implementing quantum ML models. Covers the parameter shift rule for computing exact gradients on quantum hardware — important because finite differences are too noisy on real devices.

title: Supervised quantum machine learning models are kernel methods
authors: Schuld, M., Killoran, N.
idea: Proves that all supervised quantum ML models are equivalent to kernel methods, where the kernel is defined by the inner product of quantum feature states. This unifies QML with classical kernel theory and provides rigorous tools for analyzing quantum models.
takeaway: A unifying theoretical result. Every quantum classifier is secretly a kernel method. This connects QML to the rich theory of classical kernels and makes it much easier to compare quantum models to classical baselines.

title: Variational quantum algorithms
authors: Cerezo, M., Arrasmith, A., Babbush, R., Benjamin, S. C., Endo, S., Fujii, K., McClean, J. R., Mitarai, K., Yuan, X., Cincio, L., Coles, P. J.
idea: A comprehensive survey of variational quantum algorithms — covering design, training, applications to chemistry, optimization, and ML, alongside the key challenges: barren plateaus, noise, and the difficulty of demonstrating quantum advantage.
takeaway: The most complete and balanced review of the VQA landscape as of 2021. Honest about both the promise and the deep challenges. Required reading for anyone working on near-term quantum algorithms.

title: A rigorous and robust quantum speed-up in supervised machine learning
authors: Liu, Y., Arunachalam, S., Temme, K.
idea: Provides a rigorous proof-of-principle quantum advantage in supervised ML for a specific problem based on discrete logarithm — a problem believed to be hard classically but easy quantumly. The dataset was artificially constructed to demonstrate the separation.
takeaway: The first rigorous quantum ML speedup result, but on an artificially constructed dataset. Shows that quantum advantage is possible in principle but requires data with genuine computational hardness structure — not typical ML benchmarks.

title: Data re-uploading for a universal quantum classifier
authors: Perez-Salinas, A., Cervera-Lierta, A., Gil-Fuster, E., Latorre, J. I.
idea: Shows that a single qubit can act as a universal classifier by repeatedly re-uploading classical data at multiple circuit layers, interleaved with trainable rotations. Demonstrates that quantum advantage in ML does not require many qubits — it requires the right structure.
takeaway: A surprisingly powerful result: one qubit with data re-uploading can approximate any function. Changes the intuition about what makes quantum ML models expressive — it is the encoding structure, not the qubit count.

title: Connecting ansatz expressibility to gradient magnitudes and barren plateaus
authors: Holmes, Z., Sharma, K., Cerezo, M., Coles, P. J.
idea: Proves a direct mathematical connection between circuit expressibility and barren plateaus: circuits that can approximate 2-designs (highly expressive) necessarily have exponentially vanishing gradients. The trainability-expressibility trade-off is fundamental and inescapable.
takeaway: Closes the loop on the barren plateau story. You cannot have both high expressibility and trainability in a general parametrized circuit. Any approach to fixing barren plateaus must sacrifice some expressibility.

title: Classical and quantum bounded depth approximation algorithms
authors: Hastings, M. B.
idea: Shows that for certain combinatorial optimization problems, classical algorithms match the performance of constant-depth QAOA. Challenges the assumption that shallow quantum circuits provide advantage over classical algorithms for optimization.
takeaway: Important skeptical result for QAOA. For some problems, QAOA depth p=1 or p=2 can be matched by classical algorithms. Quantum advantage in optimization likely requires deep circuits that are out of reach for NISQ devices.

title: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
authors: Acharya, R., Aleiner, I., Allen, R. et al. (Google Quantum AI)
idea: Google Willow processor demonstrates two surface code memories operating below the error correction threshold. Increasing the code distance from 5 to 7 reduces the logical error rate by a factor of 2.14. The logical qubit lifetime exceeds the best physical qubit by 2.4x.
takeaway: The most important hardware result of 2024. Below-threshold operation means adding more qubits makes the computer more reliable — the prerequisite for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
authors: Bravyi, S., Cross, A. W., Gambetta, J. M., Maslov, D., Rall, P., Yoder, T. J.
idea: Demonstrates fault-tolerant quantum memory using low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes achieving an error threshold of 0.7% on par with surface codes but with dramatically lower qubit overhead. LDPC codes can encode more logical qubits per physical qubit than surface codes.
takeaway: Surface codes require roughly 1000 physical qubits per logical qubit. LDPC codes could reduce this overhead significantly, making fault-tolerant quantum computing much more hardware-efficient.

title: Absence of barren plateaus in finite local-depth circuits with long-range entanglement
authors: Zhang, H., Wan, K., Mlynar, P., Coles, P. J., Cerezo, M.
idea: Proves that specific circuit architectures with finite local depth and long-range entanglement can avoid barren plateaus even at scale. Provides a constructive route to trainable deep quantum circuits.
takeaway: Specific architectural choices can provably avoid barren plateaus. But these architectures are restrictive and may limit expressibility — the trainability-expressibility trade-off remains.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum simulations of chemistry in first quantization
authors: Babbush, R., Berry, D. W., Jones, N. C., Gidney, C., Su, Y., McClean, J. R., Neven, H.
idea: A comprehensive resource estimation for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of industrially relevant chemistry problems. Shows that simulating molecules like FeMoco for nitrogen fixation requires millions of T gates and thousands of logical qubits.
takeaway: Quantum chemistry is the most promising practical application of quantum computing but honest resource estimates show it requires fault-tolerant hardware we do not yet have. Essential for calibrating realistic expectations about quantum advantage timelines.

title: Quantum algorithms for density functional theory with minimal readout
authors: Zhao, Y., Nishi, H., Kosugi, T., Hirose, S., Sakagami, H., Oikawa, T., Okayama, T., Matsushita, Y.
idea: Presents a qubit-efficient encoding for Kohn-Sham density functional theory wavefunctions, with a quantum algorithm that computes all occupied orbitals simultaneously. By avoiding the costly readout of the electronic density — a key bottleneck — the method enables total energy evaluation with a potential exponential speedup for the Harris functional.
takeaway: The input/output problem is what kills many claimed quantum speedups: reading data in and out of quantum states can erase any advantage. This work is interesting precisely because it sidesteps density readout entirely, attacking the real bottleneck rather than ignoring it.
featuredNote: A quantum DFT algorithm that avoids the costly readout of electronic density — directly attacking the input/output bottleneck that erases many claimed quantum speedups. A potential exponential speedup for the Harris functional.

title: Qiskit QuantumKatas: Adapting Microsoft's Quantum Computing exercises for LLM evaluation
authors: Cruz-Benito, J., Faro, I.
idea: Adapts Microsoft's QuantumKatas curriculum from Q# to Qiskit and packages it as a benchmark of 350 tasks across 26 categories with deterministic simulation-based verification. Evaluating 16 LLMs across 7 prompting setups (39,200 runs), the benchmark cleanly separates models with pass rates from 32% to 83%.
takeaway: The most revealing finding: when LLMs fail at quantum coding, the problem is usually faulty quantum reasoning, not broken syntax. Models implement known algorithms well (Simon's: 82%) but struggle to encode classical problems into quantum terms (SAT for Grover's: 34%). Quantum intuition is the hard part — for humans and machines alike.
featuredNote: A new benchmark for how well LLMs write quantum code. The striking result: models fail at quantum reasoning, not syntax — they can write valid Qiskit but get the quantum logic wrong, especially when encoding classical problems into quantum form.

title: A sharp interaction-degree threshold for simulating QAOA
authors: Āboliņš, R., Ambainis, A.
idea: Identifies a sharp interaction-degree threshold for classically simulating QAOA with 2-local cost functions. At degree 2, exact classical sampling from depth-p QAOA runs in polynomial time when p = O(log n). At degree 3, classical sampling with even small multiplicative error would collapse the polynomial hierarchy to its third level — strong evidence of genuine hardness.
takeaway: The crucial subtlety: the hard degree-3 instances have trivially optimizable cost functions, so sampling hardness does NOT imply a quantum optimization advantage. Conflating sampling hardness with optimization advantage is a common misconception — this paper draws the line precisely. Not all QAOA instances are equally quantum.
featuredNote: A sharp degree-2 vs degree-3 threshold for classically simulating QAOA, from Ambainis and Āboliņš. The key insight: even where classical sampling is hard, the cost functions are trivially optimizable — so sampling hardness alone does not prove a quantum optimization advantage.

title: Quantum-enhanced Large Language Models on Quantum Hardware via Cayley Unitary Adapters
authors: Aizpurua, B., Singh, S., Kshetrimayum, A., Jahromi, S. S., Orus, R.
idea: Inserts Cayley-parameterised unitary adapters — quantum circuit blocks — into the frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs, executed on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two. The method improves the perplexity of Llama 3.1 8B by 1.4% with only 6,000 additional parameters, with end-to-end inference validated on real quantum hardware, not a simulator.
takeaway: This is feasibility, not quantum advantage — and that distinction is the whole point. The 1.4% gain used only 6,000 parameters, but the key control (would 6,000 classical parameters do the same on the 8B model?) was only tested on a smaller 135M model. The headline is that real quantum hardware entered a production LLM's inference loop. The cold water is that it took over 4 hours for what a GPU does in under a second.
featuredNote: Real quantum hardware enters the inference loop of a production-scale LLM (Llama 3.1 8B on IBM's 156-qubit machine) — a genuine first. But read it as feasibility, not advantage: a 1.4% gain that took over 4 hours to run, where a GPU finishes in under a second.

title: Securing Elliptic Curve Cryptocurrencies against Quantum Vulnerabilities: Resource Estimates and Mitigations
authors: Babbush, R., Zalcman, A., Gidney, C., Broughton, M., Khattar, T., Neven, H., Bergamaschi, T., Drake, J., Boneh, D.
idea: Provides new resource estimates for breaking the 256-bit Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem — the core of modern blockchain cryptography. Shor's algorithm can run with under 1,450 logical qubits and under 70 million Toffoli gates; on superconducting hardware with 1e-3 error rates, the attack executes in minutes using fewer than half a million physical qubits. Introduces a fast-clock vs slow-clock architecture distinction that determines whether real-time on-spend attacks are feasible.
takeaway: Sharpens the 'quantum breaks all crypto' picture into concrete, current numbers. The threat to elliptic-curve cryptocurrencies is real and specific — but it still requires fault-tolerant hardware that does not yet exist, and post-quantum migration is already underway. The fast-clock vs slow-clock framing is what decides whether live transactions are at risk.
featuredNote: From Google Quantum AI, Stanford, and the Ethereum Foundation: concrete resource estimates for breaking elliptic-curve cryptocurrency cryptography — under 1,450 logical qubits, executable in minutes on future superconducting hardware. A sharp, current update to the 'quantum will break crypto' question, with an urgent call to migrate to post-quantum cryptography.

title: Breakeven demonstration of quantum low-density parity-check codes
authors: Tham, E., Goldman, M. L., Debnath, S., Patel, A. N., Saraladevi, J., Nguyen, J., Nielsen, E., Pisenti, N., Wright, K., Gamble, J., Delfosse, N.
idea: Demonstrates nine quantum error-correcting codes with very different connectivity requirements on a single trapped-ion device without hardware reconfiguration, spanning qLDPC, topological, and concatenated codes. A qLDPC code encoding 4 logical qubits into 18 physical qubits achieves a logical error rate up to 9x better than a prior superconducting demonstration — and reaches breakeven, where some logical qubit lifetimes meet or exceed the physical qubits.
takeaway: The experimental counterpart to qLDPC theory. These codes promise far better logical-to-physical qubit density than surface codes — directly attacking the overhead problem — but require non-local stabilizer measurements. Breakeven here is real but shown for specific code and channel combinations, not universally. A meaningful step, achieved on a stationary ion chain without physical shuttling.
featuredNote: An experimental milestone for quantum LDPC codes — the leading challenger to surface codes for fault tolerance. On a trapped-ion device, 4 logical qubits in 18 physical qubits reach breakeven, with logical error rates up to 9x better than a prior superconducting demonstration.
